docs.t: Support — help with Dlonem apps and CK3 mods
docs.x: Support Get help If you found a bug, hit a snag, or have a feature idea, I’d like to hear about it. Everything here reaches one person (me), so be as specific as you like. Email contact@dlonem.com Home › Support Where to write Anything sent to contact@dlonem.com reaches me, so if you are unsure, use that. If you already know which app you are writing about, its own address gets there a step faster. Each one is listed on that app’s privacy policy page , alongside the policy itself. Replies come from officialdlonem@gmail.com . That is us, not spam; the @dlonem.com addresses receive mail but cannot send it. For the Crusader Kings III mods, Discord is faster than email. Bug reports land in front of me and the rest of the community at the same time, and someone has usually hit your problem already: The Long Night Discord , for The Long Night & Azor Ahai Supernatural Discord , for the Supernatural mod Getting a faster answer I aim to respond within a few business days. To help me help you faster, include: The app or mod name , for example Tiny Dragon Hoard or The Long Night Your device model and Android/iOS version, or for a mod, your CK3 and AGOT versions What you expected to happen, and what happened instead For a mod, your load order and any other mods you are running (most mod problems turn out to be two mods disagreeing) A screenshot is worth several paragraphs. If an app crashed, telling me what you tapped immediately before it happened is usually the single most useful detail. Questions that come up a lot Where is my tracking data stored? On your device. The Break Buddy apps keep what you enter (history, notes and reminders) locally. I do not collect it, and I cannot read it. That is also why I cannot recover it for you if a phone is lost, which is what the in-app backup export is for. Do I need an account? No. None of the apps need an account. Tiny Dragon Hoard offers an optional Google Play Games sign-in for leaderboards and achievements; everything else works without signing in to anything. Is there a subscription? No. The apps are free, and where there is a paid unlock it is a one-time purchase. I am not going to charge you monthly for a habit tracker. I bought the unlock and changed phones. How do I get it back? Your unlock is tied to the store account you bought it with, so signing in to the same Google Play or App Store account restores it. Note that restoring one of the app’s own backup files will not carry the unlock across. Entitlement always comes from the store, never from an imported file, and the apps are written to keep it that way. When is the iOS version out? THC Break Buddy is on the App Store now. Caffeine Break Buddy, Nicotine Break Buddy and Tiny Dragon Hoard are Android-only for the moment. Each app page shows its current status on both stores. That is the page I keep up to date, so it will always be ahead of anything I could write here. A mod is not working. What should I check first? Load order and conflicting mods, in that order. Both mod pages carry their own FAQ covering load order, compatibility with other mods, and whether you need to start a new save; see The Long Night & Azor Ahai or Supernatural . If you are running both of my mods together, you also need the compatibility patch, which is explained on the mods page . Can I install the mods without Steam? Yes. Both mods have a manual download route with step-by-step instructions, linked from the mods page . Something in an app looks wrong or overlaps If text is colliding or a ring looks squashed, check your phone’s system font-size setting first. A very large display font can push layouts past what they were designed for. Tell me your font-size setting when you report it and it saves us both a round trip. Feature ideas Feature ideas are welcome, and a fair number of the things in these apps started as somebody’s email. I cannot promise a timeline, and I will tell you if something does not fit the app rather than leaving you waiting on it.

docs.t: The Game Center — a Discord server since 2016
docs.x: Est. May 2016 The Game Center The first server I ever made, and the one that turned into a community by accident. It is still running. How it started The real reason I made it In May 2016 my friend group was still calling each other on Skype, which meant somebody had to start the call and everybody had to be there for it. I found Discord before most people had heard of it, showed everyone, and they took to it immediately. I will be honest about the next part, because it is the real reason. I made the server because I wanted to be the one who owned it. I could see where this was going and I wanted to get there first. It is not a noble founding story, but it is a true one. It began as a room for fewer than fifty people to play Dota in, with a plain controller icon and no ambitions. Within a year there were two hundred and fifty of us. People brought friends, those friends brought friends, and at some point it stopped being a group chat. The first website Eight characters you cannot copy Here is a problem that sounds trivial and was not. You cannot copy and paste out of a video game. If you met someone in a match and wanted to invite them, you had to read eight random characters aloud and hope they typed them correctly. So I built a website. One page, one button. Go to the address, click join, you are in the room. That was the whole product, and it worked. I was not a web developer and it showed. That site is long gone, but the idea was right. This page is the same idea, built with more care, nine years later. The point of it Especially the quiet ones In 2017 I wrote myself a set of messages to send to people who had joined and then never said anything. It was not a moderation thing; I did not like the idea of somebody sitting in a server for months feeling like they were not part of it. One was written specifically for people who do not talk because they are shy, or because walking into a room where everyone already knows each other is hard. The gist of it: the regulars are good people, we post nonsense daily, and not knowing anyone yet should not be the thing that stops you. That is still the idea. I wanted the bar where everybody knows your name, with considerably more Dota. The hard part Keeping a room comfortable Wanting a place where quiet people feel welcome sounds simple until you have to enforce it. It started with slurs, which was easy; nobody serious argued the point. Then it was people telling each other to go kill themselves, and that is where I stopped treating any of it as banter. I brought in bots that caught those phrases, deleted the message, and sometimes removed the person with it. Then came the pushback: too much censorship. I never agreed and I still do not. What got removed was a short list of things whose only purpose is to make somebody feel small. Everything else was fair game. We opened an uncensored channel where anyone could say whatever they liked, and almost nobody used it, which told me the objection was never about wanting to say those things. A server where the loudest people set the rules is a server the quiet ones leave, without saying anything. What we did Game nights and Christmas mugs We ran Dota 2 in-house nights: twelve against twelve, any rank welcome, a voice channel per team, with fallbacks for when not enough people turned up. In hindsight they were held together with tape: I was organising instead of playing and the teams were assembled largely on vibes. They were also some of the best nights the server ever had. For four Decembers I ran holiday giveaways: mugs, shirts, stickers, and a pile of games bought out of my own pocket. No sponsor and no angle. People had been good to each other all year and it seemed like the right way to say so. I stopped after 2021, which felt like the right place to stop. The trade What it cost The server worked. That is also what broke it for the people who were there first. The original group slowly stopped showing up: too many people, too many strangers, too much noise. One of my oldest friends has never liked being in a room with people he does not know, and by then that is exactly what this was. I spent years pushing to get more people in, which was the same act as pushing my friends out. I did not see it that way at the time. So I made them a smaller, private one instead, and that is the one they still use. Which brings me back to owning things. I like making things I control (servers, apps, mods, this website). I hardly ever use the power, but I like having it, because I do not entirely trust other people with it. That is why it took me so long to hand anyone else the keys, and why some of the drama that eventually split the server was other people wanting exactly the same thing. Nine years on A tenth of a percent Someone who joined here as a teenager and left for college once told me this was the server he grew up in. You cannot design that. You can only leave the door open long enough for it to happen to somebody. I figure I own about a tenth of a percent of a lot of people's brains. Somebody mentions Discord servers, and somewhere out there a person goes: oh, The Game Center — yeah, I used to be in that. It happened almost entirely because I would not stop asking people to join. The door is still open If that invite ever stops working, this one goes to the same place. The other rooms There are three more The Game Center is the oldest of four Discord servers I run, and the rest are on the Community page . Dlonem's Den goes with the YouTube channel ; the other two are for my Crusader Kings III mods, The Long Night & Azor Ahai and Supernatural .
